note: Subjects/9701 Chemistry/11 Group 17/11.3 Some reactions of the halide ions.md
outline: Halide ions become stronger reducing agents down Group 17. Aqueous silver ions give AgCl (white), AgBr (cream) and AgI (yellow); ammonia dissolves AgCl when dilute, AgBr when concentrated, but not AgI. Concentrated sulfuric acid first protonates solid halides. Bromide and iodide then reduce the acid: bromide gives bromine and sulfur dioxide, while iodide can give iodine and sulfur dioxide, sulfur or hydrogen sulfide.

misconceptions.statement: Chloride is the strongest reducing halide.
misconceptions.refutation: Iodide loses electrons most readily, so reducing strength increases down Group 17.
misconceptions.contrast: Oxidising strength of the halogens decreases down the group.

misconceptions.statement: Concentrated sulfuric acid oxidises chloride to chlorine.
misconceptions.refutation: Chloride undergoes proton transfer only; HCl forms without chlorine.
misconceptions.contrast: Bromide and iodide also reduce sulfuric acid.

misconceptions.statement: All silver halides dissolve in dilute ammonia.
misconceptions.refutation: AgCl dissolves in dilute ammonia; AgBr requires concentrated ammonia; AgI remains insoluble.
misconceptions.contrast: Precipitate colours are white, cream and yellow respectively.

misconceptions.statement: Bromide gives a white silver halide precipitate.
misconceptions.refutation: AgBr is cream; white is AgCl.

misconceptions.statement: Iodide must produce sulfur dioxide, sulfur and hydrogen sulfide together in every reaction with concentrated sulfuric acid.
misconceptions.refutation: Write the pathway specified by the evidence. Different extents of sulfur reduction are possible; no single experiment must show them all.
misconceptions.contrast: Possible sulfur oxidation states are plus four, zero and minus two; the observed pathway depends on conditions.

items.stem: An aqueous mixture of sodium chloride and sodium bromide is acidified with dilute nitric acid and treated with excess aqueous silver nitrate. The precipitate formed is filtered off, washed, and then shaken with excess dilute aqueous ammonia. What remains at the end?

items.explanation: Excess silver nitrate precipitates both halides: $\ce{AgCl}$ (white) and $\ce{AgBr}$ (cream). Dilute ammonia dissolves $\ce{AgCl}$ only; $\ce{AgBr}$ needs concentrated ammonia, so the cream $\ce{AgBr}$ is left behind. No iodide was present, so no yellow $\ce{AgI}$ can form.
hints: Decide first which silver halides the excess silver nitrate can precipitate here.

items.stem: Concentrated sulfuric acid is added separately to solid sodium chloride and to solid sodium iodide. Which statement correctly compares the sulfur-containing products of the two reactions?

options.B: Only sodium iodide reduces the sulfuric acid, giving a reduced sulfur species such as $\ce{SO2}$, $\ce{S}$ or $\ce{H2S}$.
options.C: Only sodium chloride reduces the sulfuric acid, giving chlorine gas and $\ce{SO2}$.
options.D: Neither solid changes the oxidation number of sulfur, because no halide ion can reduce sulfuric acid.

items.explanation: Both solids first undergo proton transfer to give the hydrogen halide, so steamy fumes of $\ce{HCl}$ and of $\ce{HI}$ appear in each case. Iodide is a strong enough reducing agent to reduce the acid further, to $\ce{SO2}$, $\ce{S}$ or $\ce{H2S}$, with iodine formed; chloride is too weak a reducing agent, so no chlorine and no reduced sulfur species form.
hints: Both reactions begin with the same kind of step, before any redox.
Ask which halide ion loses an electron readily enough to reduce sulfur from $+6$.
Write the acid-base equation for each solid first.

9701-11.3.1.motivate: Why can iodide turn bromine into bromide, while bromide cannot turn iodine into iodide? The answer is the halide ions' different willingness to give away electrons.
9701-11.3.1.establish: A reducing agent donates electrons and is oxidised. The relative reactivity of halide ions as reducing agents increases down Group 17: $\ce{F- < Cl- < Br- < I-}$. Thus iodide is a stronger reducing agent than bromide, which is stronger than chloride. In a reaction such as $\ce{2I- -> I2 + 2e-}$, iodide loses electrons. Consequently iodide can reduce bromine to bromide, but bromide cannot reduce iodine. This reducing trend is the reverse of the oxidising trend of the halogens. Concentrated sulfuric acid illustrates the trend: chloride undergoes only acid-base reaction, bromide also reduces the acid to sulfur dioxide, and iodide can reduce it further, even to hydrogen sulfide.
9701-11.3.1.connect: Use the trend to predict whether a halide will reduce a halogen or concentrated sulfuric acid. Name the halide as the reducing agent when it loses electrons.
9701-11.3.1.note:
- Halide-ion reducing strength: $\ce{F- < Cl- < Br- < I-}$.
- A reducing agent loses electrons and is oxidised.
- Iodide can reduce sulfuric acid more extensively than bromide; chloride does not reduce it.
9701-11.3.1.self_explain: Why does bromide form bromine with concentrated sulfuric acid but chloride does not form chlorine?
9701-11.3.1.plain_words: Start from electron transfer: oxidation means losing electrons, and a reducing agent supplies those electrons to another species. Halide ions lower in Group 17 have more occupied shells, greater ionic radius and more shielding. Their outer electrons experience weaker attraction to the nucleus and are lost more readily, despite the greater nuclear charge. Reducing strength therefore increases down the group. Keep the particles distinct: halide ions donate electrons, whereas halogen molecules accept electrons; halogen oxidising strength decreases down the group.

terms.meaning: A negatively charged ion of a halogen with one extra electron.
An electron donor that is itself oxidised.
terms.spoken: two X minus ions form X two and two electrons

terms.meaning: A measure of ion size; the outer electrons are further from the nucleus in larger halide ions.
Inner electrons reduce the attraction felt by outer electrons from the nucleus.
An electron acceptor that is itself reduced.
terms.spoken: X two accepts two electrons to form two X minus ions

forms.name: Predict a halide–halogen redox direction
wordings: Predict whether a halide reduces a halogen and explain your choice.
Write a balanced ionic equation and identify the reducing agent.
forms.example:
Worked example: compare bromine water added to aqueous sodium iodide with iodine added to aqueous sodium bromide.
1. Identify the donor as a halide ion and the acceptor as a halogen molecule. Iodide is a stronger reducing agent than bromide.
2. Write the electron loss: $\ce{2I-(aq) -> I2(aq) + 2e-}$. Write the electron gain: $\ce{Br2(aq) + 2e- -> 2Br-(aq)}$.
3. Cancel electrons: $\ce{Br2(aq) + 2I-(aq) -> 2Br-(aq) + I2(aq)}$. Iodide is oxidised and is the reducing agent; bromine is reduced and is the oxidising agent.
4. Reversing the reagents does not give displacement: bromide cannot reduce iodine under these aqueous conditions.
forms.check: Chlorine water is added to aqueous potassium iodide. Predict whether displacement occurs, write the balanced ionic equation with states and name both agents. Explain why iodide loses electrons more readily than chloride using radius and shielding.
forms.answer: Displacement occurs: $\ce{Cl2(aq) + 2I-(aq) -> 2Cl-(aq) + I2(aq)}$. Iodide is the reducing agent and chlorine is the oxidising agent. Iodide has a larger ionic radius and more inner-shell shielding than chloride, so its outer electrons experience weaker nuclear attraction and are lost more readily.

rubric.point: Predict displacement of iodide by chlorine.
Give the balanced ionic equation with states: one aqueous chlorine molecule and two aqueous iodide ions form two aqueous chloride ions and one aqueous iodine molecule.
Identify iodide as the reducing agent: it loses electrons.
Identify chlorine as the oxidising agent: it gains electrons.
Iodide has greater radius and shielding than chloride, giving weaker attraction and easier electron loss.

misconceptions.fix: Ask whether electrons are being gained or lost. Halide reducing strength increases down the group; halogen oxidising strength decreases.

9701-11.3.2.motivate: Three colourless halide solutions can be distinguished by the colour of their silver precipitates and their responses to ammonia. A dry salt's reaction with concentrated sulfuric acid gives a second line of evidence.
9701-11.3.2.establish: With aqueous silver ions, $\ce{Ag+(aq) + X-(aq) -> AgX(s)}$. Chloride gives white $\ce{AgCl}$, which dissolves in dilute aqueous ammonia. Bromide gives cream $\ce{AgBr}$, which dissolves in concentrated ammonia but not dilute ammonia. Iodide gives yellow $\ce{AgI}$, insoluble even in concentrated ammonia. Ammonia lowers the free silver-ion concentration through complex formation, allowing some precipitates to dissolve; the complex formula is not required. Solid halides first undergo acid-base reaction with concentrated sulfuric acid, for example $\ce{NaCl + H2SO4 -> NaHSO4 + HCl}$. Chloride stops there. Bromide also reduces sulfuric acid: $\ce{2HBr + H2SO4 -> Br2 + SO2 + 2H2O}$. Iodide produces iodine and can give $\ce{SO2}$, sulfur or $\ce{H2S}$: $\ce{2HI + H2SO4 -> I2 + SO2 + 2H2O}$; $\ce{6HI + H2SO4 -> 3I2 + S + 4H2O}$; $\ce{8HI + H2SO4 -> 4I2 + H2S + 4H2O}$.
9701-11.3.2.connect: The stronger reducing power down Group 17 explains the increasingly extensive reduction of sulfuric acid. The silver test distinguishes the ions through precipitation and ammonia solubility.
9701-11.3.2.note:
- $\ce{AgCl}$ white, dissolves in dilute ammonia.
- $\ce{AgBr}$ cream, dissolves in concentrated ammonia.
- $\ce{AgI}$ yellow, insoluble in ammonia.
- Chloride gives HCl only with concentrated sulfuric acid; bromide and iodide also cause redox.
9701-11.3.2.self_explain: A cream precipitate dissolves only in concentrated ammonia. Which halide ion was present, and how would it react with concentrated sulfuric acid?
9701-11.3.2.plain_words: Use two separate methods. For identification, use an aqueous sample, add dilute nitric acid before aqueous silver nitrate, and record the precipitate colour. Then test the precipitate with dilute ammonia and, if it remains, sufficiently concentrated ammonia in excess. White silver chloride dissolves in dilute ammonia, cream silver bromide requires concentrated ammonia, and yellow silver iodide remains. For a solid halide with concentrated sulfuric acid, first recognise proton transfer to form a hydrogen halide; only then decide whether electron transfer follows. Sulfur may be reduced to different products by iodide: these are possible pathways, not a requirement that every product appears in every experiment.

forms.name: Identify halides from silver nitrate and successive ammonia observations
wordings: Describe the reagent sequence and deduce the halide ions present.
Explain the precipitate and its behaviour in dilute and concentrated ammonia.
forms.example:
Worked example: a solution contains one of chloride, bromide or iodide. A cream precipitate forms with silver nitrate after acidification.
1. Start with the aqueous sample. Add dilute nitric acid, then aqueous silver nitrate; acidification comes before precipitation.
2. Record cream solid, not a cream solution: $\ce{Ag+(aq) + Br-(aq) -> AgBr(s)}$.
3. The solid remains in dilute aqueous ammonia but dissolves in excess concentrated aqueous ammonia, giving a colourless solution.
4. The two observations together identify bromide. Colour alone is less reliable than colour combined with ammonia behaviour.
forms.check: An aqueous sample contains exactly two of chloride, bromide and iodide, with no other precipitating ions. Describe the acidification and precipitation reagents in order. Some precipitate dissolves in excess dilute ammonia; after treating the remaining solid with excess concentrated ammonia a yellow residue remains. Identify the two halides and the residue, explain both ammonia observations, and write the two precipitation equations with states.
forms.answer: Add dilute nitric acid, then aqueous silver nitrate. Chloride and iodide are present. Silver chloride dissolves in dilute ammonia; silver iodide remains as the yellow residue even in concentrated ammonia. Bromide is excluded because exactly two halides are present and both have been identified. $\ce{Ag+(aq) + Cl-(aq) -> AgCl(s)}$ and $\ce{Ag+(aq) + I-(aq) -> AgI(s)}$. Do not infer composition from the blended initial colour.

rubric.point: Use an aqueous sample; add dilute nitric acid before aqueous silver nitrate.
Identify chloride because silver chloride dissolves in dilute ammonia.
Identify iodide and the yellow residue as silver iodide, insoluble even in concentrated ammonia.
Give the balanced precipitation equation for chloride with aqueous silver and chloride ions and solid silver chloride.
Give the balanced precipitation equation for iodide with aqueous silver and iodide ions and solid silver iodide.

forms.name: Distinguish acid–base and redox with concentrated sulfuric acid
wordings: Write separate acid–base and redox equations and identify the agents.
Use oxidation numbers to distinguish possible sulfur products from compulsory observations.
forms.example:
Worked example: explain the reaction of solid sodium bromide with concentrated sulfuric acid.
1. First form hydrogen bromide by proton transfer: $\ce{NaBr(s) + H2SO4(l) -> NaHSO4(s) + HBr(g)}$. Bromine stays at $-1$ and sulfur stays at $+6$: this step is acid–base, not redox.
2. Hydrogen bromide then reduces sulfuric acid: $\ce{2HBr(g) + H2SO4(l) -> Br2(g) + SO2(g) + 2H2O(l)}$. Reddish-brown bromine is formed.
3. Bromine changes from $-1$ to $0$; two bromide ions lose two electrons overall. Sulfur changes from $+6$ to $+4$, gaining two electrons. This checks the balanced redox step.
4. Bromide (or hydrogen bromide) is the reducing agent; sulfuric acid is the oxidising agent in this second step. The acid therefore has different roles in the two steps.
forms.check: In one possible reaction of iodide with concentrated sulfuric acid, sulfate is reduced to hydrogen sulfide and iodide is oxidised to iodine. In acidic conditions, write balanced ionic half-equations for these two changes, then state how many iodide ions supply the electrons needed to reduce one sulfate ion. Identify the oxidising and reducing agents. State symbols are not required.
forms.answer: Reduction: $\ce{SO4^2- + 10H+ + 8e- -> H2S + 4H2O}$. Oxidation: $\ce{2I- -> I2 + 2e-}$. Eight iodide ions supply eight electrons per sulfate ion. Sulfuric acid (or sulfate) is the oxidising agent and iodide (or hydrogen iodide) is the reducing agent. Equivalent balanced multiples are acceptable.

rubric.point: Give a balanced sulfate-to-hydrogen sulfide reduction half-equation in acid, with eight electrons on the left; accept equivalent balanced multiples.
Give a balanced iodide-to-iodine oxidation half-equation with electrons on the right; accept equivalent balanced multiples.
State eight iodide ions supply the electrons to reduce one sulfate ion.
Identify sulfuric acid or sulfate as oxidising agent and iodide or hydrogen iodide as reducing agent.

misconceptions.temptation: Remember that ammonia dissolves one silver precipitate and apply it to every halide.
misconceptions.fix: Specify concentration: dilute dissolves silver chloride, concentrated is needed for silver bromide, and silver iodide remains.

misconceptions.idea: Concentrated sulfuric acid oxidises chloride to chlorine.
misconceptions.temptation: Assume any reaction with an oxidising acid must be redox.
misconceptions.fix: Check oxidation numbers: forming hydrogen chloride transfers a proton and leaves chlorine at minus one.

misconceptions.idea: Iodide must produce sulfur dioxide, sulfur and hydrogen sulfide together in every reaction with concentrated sulfuric acid.
misconceptions.temptation: Treat the list of possible reduction products as a compulsory observation list.
misconceptions.fix: Write the pathway specified by the evidence. Different extents of sulfur reduction are possible; no single experiment must show them all.
